turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Here's the counterintuitive thing about starting a business from scratch: the first one to three years are mostly spent solving problems that every existing business in your target market already solved. You're not building your proposition — you're proving it can exist at all.

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: That's exactly the ETA framing. Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition means you skip that. You buy a business with existing customers, proven cash flow, and operating history, and you start on day one. The 'year zero' problem — no revenue, unvalidated assumptions, customers who don't know you exist — is already behind you.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why is this a real career path now, rather than just something the occasional person does?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: The structural backdrop changed. Roughly six million US small businesses are expected to change ownership by 2035 as Baby Boomer owners retire. That's $5 trillion in enterprise value, and per the 2026 State of Main Street report, 70% of those owners have no formal succession plan. Stanford, Harvard, and INSEAD now run dedicated ETA programs. The infrastructure caught up with the opportunity.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That succession gap — does that mean buyers are competing against private equity for all of these?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Often not, and that's one of the underappreciated dynamics. A lot of retiring founders actively prefer selling to an individual operator who will preserve what they built and protect existing employees. Relationship and trust genuinely factor into who gets first access. Price is not the only variable — you're not purely competing against institutional capital.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So what are the two structural ways into this?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Funded search versus self-funded. In a funded search, you raise capital from investors, they back your search and the acquisition itself, and you end up with roughly 20 to 30 percent equity. Self-funded, often using SBA financing, means you keep full ownership but you're personally guaranteeing a leveraged balance sheet. Same destination — buy and operate a profitable business — fundamentally different risk profiles.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Stanford tracks funded search fund returns at 35.1% IRR across 681 funds. That's a genuinely strong number.

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: It is — materially better than early-stage venture capital on a risk-adjusted basis. But read the other number alongside it: more than half of searches fail to close a deal at all. The return profile for deals that do close is excellent. The base rate of actually closing is genuinely uncertain. It's a multi-year undertaking with real attrition.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Once you're searching, what actually matters in screening?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Every serious ETA source converges on two things: recurring revenue percentage and owner-independence. A business with 80% recurring revenue and a management team that runs without the founder is a completely different acquisition than one where 80% is project work and the founder's personal relationships generate every dollar.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why are those two specifically the hardest to verify?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Because the seller has natural incentive to overstate both. '80% recurring' might sit on month-to-month contracts with a single large customer. The 'strong management team' might dissolve the moment the founder's personal referral network stops feeding it. The article's rule is that every material claim needs corroboration from at least two sources independent of the seller — contracts, customer interviews, financial statements.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: A practical one on owner-independence: what's the diagnostic question that actually surfaces it?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Walk through a specific week on day 31 post-close. If the answer is 'the seller' more than twice, the business is not yet independent. Undocumented processes are another signal — a business that depends on someone's head knowledge depends on that person.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does AI fit into the ETA process?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: The highest-leverage application is first-pass diligence. Feeding financial statements, lease agreements, and contracts into a structured analysis session with explicit instructions to flag inconsistencies and owner-dependency signals compresses the review dramatically. A 2026 practitioner-benchmarked figure puts AI-assisted contract review at roughly 10 times a manual pass.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That speed sounds like it could become a liability.

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: That's the speed trap. An AI-surfaced finding is a hypothesis to verify independently, not a conclusion. And at the decision stage — before any LOI, before exclusivity — you still need a real accountant and an M&A advisor. AI compresses the research time. It does not replace the professional judgment a real transaction warrants.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What about sourcing — are the best deals on public listing platforms?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Often not. The best deals are frequently not publicly listed. Direct outreach to owners who fit your profile, with a message that's evidently specific and researched rather than templated, tends to surface less competitive deals. A retiring owner deciding who to trust with their life's work responds very differently to a genuine, researched note than to something generic.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's the sequence that actually produces better deals?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Write the buy box first, stress-test it against real market data, source beyond public listings, use AI to screen fast across many opportunities, then reserve deep diligence for the small number that clear the bar. Time spent deeply diligencing a deal that fails the buy box is wasted. Screen fast, diligence deep only on finalists.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What goes in a buy box?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Industry, revenue range, geography, your recurring revenue floor, owner-dependency tolerance, deal size relative to your actual financing capacity. Specific things, written down. The discipline that catches bad deals is the constraint you set before finding any particular deal — not the diligence you run after you've already fallen in love with one.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So the buy box is the guardrail that protects you from yourself.

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: Exactly. The article's phrasing is: don't engage with any deal that fails two or more of your criteria. The most dangerous deals aren't the obvious bad ones — they're the ones that almost fit. The buy box is how you keep 'almost' from becoming a binding commitment.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's the bottom line for someone who wants to take ETA seriously?

turns.speaker: expert
turns.text: The structural window is genuinely open — six million businesses, $5 trillion, 70% without a plan. Write the buy box before you look at a single listing. Use AI to compress the sourcing and first-pass research. Verify every material claim from two sources independent of the seller. And bring in a real accountant, advisor, and lawyer before anything binding. In that order, without skipping steps.
